title: Remove a stripped Phillips screw
mechanism_check: A Phillips cams out when the driver tip is worn, undersized, or tilted — the cross recess rounds into a cone.
Check first whether the screw is threaded into wood, metal, or a nut behind: the extraction force differs.
improvised_tools: A rubber band laid across the recess for grip; steel wool works too.
A larger Phillips or a flathead that wedges across two opposite wings.
Superglue a sacrificial driver bit into the recess (last resort before drilling).
steps: Press down hard with the correct-size driver and turn slowly — most 'stripped' screws just need axial pressure.
Lay a wide rubber band over the recess and drive through it.
Try one size up Phillips, or a flathead wedged diagonally across the cross.
As a last resort: glue a cheap bit in with superglue, wait 5 minutes, turn.
stop_conditions: Head shearing off: stop and switch to a broken-head extraction approach.
Screw in hardened metal with threadlocker: heat or proper extractors beat improvisation.

title: Remove a rounded hex/Allen bolt
mechanism_check: Hex sockets round when the key is undersized, metric/standard is mixed up, or the bolt is seized.
Confirm the socket size: a 5mm key in a 3/16 socket is the classic mismatch.
improvised_tools: A Torx bit one size up, tapped in with a hammer — the star points bite the rounded walls.
A flathead screwdriver hammered across the socket as a chisel-driver.
Penetrating oil on the threads, 15 minutes, plus hammer taps on the bolt head.
steps: Soak the threads with penetrating oil and tap the head to shock it.
Tap in the next-size-up Torx bit until it seats firmly.
Turn with steady pressure, keeping the bit perfectly straight.
If the head is proud of the surface, rag-wrapped locking pliers on the outside work too.
stop_conditions: Bolt head snapping: stop and treat it as a broken stud.
Torx spinning freely: the socket is fully wallowed — move to drilling/extractor territory.

title: Back out a broken bolt stub
mechanism_check: A stub with any exposed thread can be gripped; a stub flush or below the surface needs drilling.
Left-hand thread direction check: some studs are reverse-threaded.
improvised_tools: Locking pliers (vise-grips) clamped hard on any exposed stub.
Two nuts jammed together on the stub to make a turning head.
Penetrating oil + heat on the surrounding part (not the stub) to expand the female threads.
steps: Soak with penetrating oil; heat the surrounding metal, not the stub.
If thread is exposed: jam two nuts together on it and turn the inner nut.
If only a nub: clamp locking pliers as tight as possible, rock back and forth.
Patience over force — a quarter-turn of progress, re-oil, repeat.
stop_conditions: Stub flush or below the surface: improvisation ends here; it needs a drilled extractor.
Surrounding part is aluminum and you're heating it: stop before you anneal or warp it.

title: Remove a rusted nut without penetrating oil
mechanism_check: Rust locks threads by expanding iron oxide in the thread valleys; the bond breaks with shock, heat, or a substitute penetrant.
Check whether the bolt shank can be held — a spinning bolt defeats every nut trick.
improvised_tools: 50/50 automatic-transmission-fluid and acetone (better than most store penetrants); diesel or kerosene as a weaker substitute.
Heat from a propane torch or heat gun on the nut only, then cold water quench to crack rust.
A 6-point socket (not 12-point) or a tight box wrench — never an adjustable on a rusted nut.
steps: Soak the threads with the ATF/acetone mix; tap the nut flats with a hammer.
Heat the nut (not the bolt) for a minute, quench with water, repeat twice.
Fit a 6-point socket fully seated and turn with smooth pressure.
Work it out an eighth-turn, back in a sixteenth, re-soak — walk it off.
stop_conditions: Nut corners rounding: stop and switch to a nut-splitter or locking pliers before it's smooth.
Bolt shank twisting with the nut: hold the shank or the whole fastener will shear.

title: Drive a screw with no matching driver
mechanism_check: Match the driver to the recess pattern (Phillips, Torx, hex, Robertson) and size — the pattern is the spec, not the tool brand.
For removal, any bit that fills the recess without slop will work.
improvised_tools: Flathead screwdriver across a Phillips cross (diagonal wedge).
Hex key shank or nail in a hex socket; Torx bit in a hex socket one size down.
A coin edge in a large slotted screw; a sturdy butter knife for light-duty slots.
steps: Pick the substitute that fills the recess with the least slop.
Apply strong downward pressure — cam-out is the enemy, not torque.
Turn slowly; re-seat the substitute every quarter-turn.
For final tightening, finish with the proper driver when you get one.
stop_conditions: Recess starting to round: stop and get the right bit — a stripped recess costs more than the wait.
High-torque structural fasteners: substitutes are for removal/triage, not final torque.

title: Remove a one-way security screw
mechanism_check: One-way screws drive in but cam out on removal — the slots are ramped on one side.
Confirm it's actually one-way and not just a damaged Phillips.
improvised_tools: A flathead bit with the tip ground/filed to match the ramp angle, or two small flatheads used as a fork.
A rubber band for grip on lightly-set screws.
Left-hand grip: sometimes a tight-fitting driver turned counterclockwise with heavy pressure walks them out.
steps: Try heavy downward pressure with the best-fitting driver first — shallow one-ways often yield.
Cut a fresh straight slot across the head with a rotary tool or hacksaw blade if the head is accessible.
Drive the new slot with a flathead.
Replace with a standard screw on reinstall.
stop_conditions: Screw is in a tamper-evident security device you don't own: stop — defeating it may be unlawful.
Head too small or recessed to slot: extractors, not improvisation.

title: Free a seized machine screw with heat
mechanism_check: Seized by corrosion or threadlocker: threadlocker softens with heat (~250C), corrosion breaks with differential expansion.
Check what surrounds the screw — heat near plastic, wiring, or fuel is a different job.
improvised_tools: A soldering iron held on the screw head (precise, low collateral heat).
Heat gun or hair dryer for threadlocker; propane torch for heavy corrosion on bare metal.
Penetrating oil applied after heating, as the joint cools and draws oil in.
steps: Clear flammables and check what's behind/around the screw.
Heat the screw head (soldering iron) or the surrounding female part (torch) for 1-2 minutes.
Let it cool slightly, apply penetrating oil to the thread line.
Turn with the correct driver and firm downward pressure.
stop_conditions: Any fuel, gas line, or battery within heat range: stop — no improvised heat near combustibles.
Plastic housing softening: stop, you're melting the part that holds the threads.

title: Remove a stripped Torx screw
mechanism_check: Torx strips when the bit is a size small or the screw is seized; the star points round into a circle.
Verify the size with a proper bit first — T25 in a T27 recess is the usual culprit.
improvised_tools: Next-size-up Torx bit tapped in with a hammer.
A flathead wedged between two opposite points of the star.
Superglue + sacrificial bit for screws that must come out intact.
steps: Soak threads with penetrating oil if there's any corrosion.
Tap the next-size-up Torx in until it bites on all points.
Turn slowly with straight, heavy pressure.
If it slips, cut a straight slot across the head and use a flathead.
stop_conditions: Bit spinning freely in a fully rounded recess: move to extractor/drilling.
Screw head snapping under hammer taps: switch to broken-stub methods.

title: Tighten a spinning nut in a blind cavity
mechanism_check: The nut spins because nothing holds it — you need to jam the nut while turning the bolt from the accessible side.
Feel for the nut shape through the cavity: hex nuts can be wedged, square nuts too.
improvised_tools: A flat screwdriver or putty knife wedged against a nut flat to jam it.
Sticky tack, chewing gum, or tape on a fingertip/stick to hold the nut in place.
A small magnet on a stick to position and hold a steel nut.
steps: Reach in and press a screwdriver blade against one flat of the nut.
Turn the bolt slowly from the front while keeping wedge pressure on the nut.
Once threads catch, the nut will usually pull itself against the back of the cavity.
For reassembly, stick the nut to the screwdriver with tack to position it.
stop_conditions: Cavity too deep to reach or see: stop fishing blind — open access or use a borescope.
Nut is a captive/clip nut that's broken free: the retainer needs replacing, not jamming.

title: Extract a screw with a broken-off head
mechanism_check: Head snapped from over-torque or corrosion; the shank remains threaded in the hole.
If any shank protrudes, grip methods work; if flush, you need to cut a new drive.
improvised_tools: Locking pliers on any protruding shank.
A rotary tool or hacksaw blade to cut a straight slot in a flush shank.
Penetrating oil on the threads before any turning.
steps: Soak the threads with penetrating oil.
Protruding shank: clamp locking pliers tight and rock it out.
Flush shank: cut a clean straight slot across the top and drive it with a flathead.
Turn counterclockwise; work back and forth if it's tight.
stop_conditions: Shank below the surface with nothing to grip or slot: this is drill-and-extractor work now.
Shank in brittle cast material: snapping it flush inside means a much harder job — go slow.
